parole.testo: From Middle Low German dûne, from Old Norse dúnn. The diphthong -au- is a secondary adaptation from the Low German to the standard German vowel system.

parole.significato: cod (marine fish of the family Gadidae)
parole.testo: From Middle High German dorsch, borrowed from Middle Low German dorsch, itself from Old Norse þorskr, from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz.

16th century, from Middle Low German *hummer, itself from Old Norse humarr, perhaps through early Norwegian (as many lobsters were caught off the coast of Norway). From the same North Germanic source Modern Low German Hummer, Plautdietsch Humma, Dutch hommer.

parole.significato: keel (beam at the underside of a ship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kēl, kil, probably borrowed from Old Norse kjǫlr. Compare Dutch kiel, English keel.
Borrowed from Middle Low German rif, ref, from Old Norse rif.
Borrowed from Middle Low German schorbuk, probably from Old Norse skyrbjúgr. Doublet of Skorbut.

parole.significato: skra (kind of medieval legal document in northern Germany and around the Baltic Sea)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schrā, itself probably from Old Norse skrá (“parchment”), though it might also be inherited from the underlying Proto-Germanic *skrahō.

16th century, calque of Middle Low German vēlvrât (“wolverine”, literally “glutton”), also vēlvras, vēlvratz (this last being the earliest attested form in 1498). Further in all likelihood a folk-etymological alteration of Old Norse *fjallfress ~ *fellfross (literally “mountain cat”), from fjall, fe
